overview: This bill, the Iran Human Rights, Internet Freedom, and Accountability Act of 2026, aims to help people in Iran get around government censorship and internet shutdowns and to support human rights there. It makes the Secretary of State the lead official for promoting internet freedom in Iran, requires an updated strategy covering tools such as VPNs (apps that hide and route around blocked connections) and direct-to-phone satellite service, and extends an existing Iran internet freedom grant program through 2030. It directs the State Department to support low-cost technologies that can overcome blackouts, write a strategy to support independent Iranian journalists and civil society, and set up cybersecurity training for activists. The Government Accountability Office, Congress's watchdog, would review spending on Iran-related democracy programs. The bill states it does not authorize military force or any transaction barred by sanctions laws without a license. As of July 27, 2026, the Senate Foreign Relations Committee had approved an amended version and it was awaiting a vote by the full Senate.
for: Supporters say keeping Iranians connected to each other and the outside world is one of the most direct ways to support their human rights, especially when the government cuts off the internet during protests.
against: Critics say outside technology efforts may have limited reach against a government determined to control communications, and that U.S.-backed tools could put users at risk or be portrayed by Iran's government as foreign interference.
